name: role-object
intent: Let a key abstraction present different context-specific interfaces by attaching role objects to a shared core at runtime, so each client context sees only the interface it needs while the subject keeps one identity and one integrated state.
problem: One entity legitimately has to play different roles for different clients: each context needs a context-specific interface on the same logical object, and the set of roles changes at runtime. Integrating every context-specific operation into the key abstraction bloats its interface for all clients, while modelling each role as a subclass gives every role instance its own identity and its own copy of the shared state - so polymorphic searches return duplicates and shared attributes must be kept consistent by hand.
context: Entity- and party-centric systems shared by several applications or departments (banking, enterprise, healthcare, workflow), where context-specific views must be attached to and removed from a key abstraction at runtime and one logical object must back several concurrently played roles. It presumes objects with references and dynamic dispatch, or a viable emulation of them, and it works best when clients can request roles by specification instead of naming concrete role classes.
benefits: The key abstraction keeps a stable, context-free interface while context-specific operations live in role classes, so no client has to wade through another context's operations and localized context changes no longer force recompilation of every client.
Roles attach and detach at runtime and combine freely: a subject plays several roles at once, the same role is played by many subjects, and a new role needs no new subclass of the core.

Core and roles form one logical object with integrated state and identity: shared attributes stay on the core, role-specific state stays on the role, and role views of the same core can be recognized as conceptually identical.

Role creation is decoupled from the core through specification objects and a role trader/registry, so new roles are added without modifying the core and clients never learn how roles are instantiated.

Different contexts - even separate applications - are decoupled from each other: the loan department sees a Borrower view and the investment department an Investor view, and neither interface leaks into the other.
tradeoffs: Role-specific calls stop being ordinary compile-time-checked method calls: clients must ask the core for a role by specification and then cast or type-check the result, so the compiler can no longer verify the whole protocol.
Every role must forward the core's operations (the Decorator cost): role classes duplicate forwarding code, and every change to the core interface ripples through all of them.

Core and role state must be kept consistent explicitly - changing a core attribute may require notifying or flagging affected roles - and identity comparison needs special operations, because one logical object is represented by several technical objects.
Role combinations and migrations cannot be expressed in the type structure: constraints such as 'Borrower requires a Customer role' and valid add/remove sequences must be enforced by hand at runtime.

Ownership and lifetime are subtle: the core owns its roles and must destroy them with itself, roles must not outlive or be created without their core, and the bidirectional core-to-role-to-core reference is a cycle that burdens reference-counted runtimes and manual memory management.

participants.responsibility: Declares the common interface of the key abstraction plus the role-management protocol (add, remove, test and query roles by specification); clients program against it and ask it for role views.
Implements the Component interface and the role protocol, creates ConcreteRole instances through the role trader, and owns and manages the role objects it hands out.
Abstract superclass of every role; stores a reference to its ComponentCore and implements the Component interface by forwarding core operations to it, so a role can be used wherever the core can.
Models one context-specific view (Borrower, Investor) with its own state and operations; instantiated only by the core, and always with a core attached.

Specification-keyed creator registry that maps each role specification (class object, string, enum) to the creator that instantiates the matching ConcreteRole, keeping the core free of concrete role references.

use_cases: Banking: one customer plays Borrower, Investor and Guarantor at the same time, while the loan, investment and credit departments each see only their own role interface (the paper's GEBOS motivation).
Enterprise and party modelling: a company acts as supplier, customer, agent and regulatory counterparty for different systems, with roles added and retired over time (Fowler's roles example).
Workforce systems: an employee plays engineer, manager, salesman or retiree roles that change over a career and must be visible to different subsystems.
Compiler and language tooling: AST nodes acquire context-specific views (typing view, code-generation view, formatting view) during compilation and shed them again (a known use in the paper).
Document lifecycle: a document presents draft, review, translation and archival views as roles that come and go, each with its own operations, while remaining one document.
Runtime capability attachment: a session or user object gains temporary roles (impersonation, delegated authority) and exposes only the corresponding interface while the role is held.

Open-source reference implementation: the iluwatar/java-design-patterns role-object module transcribes the pattern directly - a Customer interface with addRole/hasRole/remRole/getRole, a CustomerCore owning its role set, a Role enum acting as the specification that maps each role to its creator, and BorrowerRole/InvestorRole extending an abstract CustomerRole.

Refactoring toolchains: the intoJ 'Introduce Role Objects' Eclipse plugin rewrites role-subclass hierarchies (Employee extends Person) into Role Object structures whose roles share state and identity with a core - and its authors report that the full delegation code is hard to understand and maintain, which is why they also ship a Lightweight Role Objects variant.

Python runtime-role libraries: amolenaar/roles (in the PEAK ObjectRoles lineage) assigns and revokes role objects on individual instances at runtime while the underlying data object keeps one state and identity - the Role Object core in a dynamic-language, DCI-style form.
avoid_when: The role set is small, stable and known at design time, and significant rules govern role combinations: make the roles subtypes of one interface instead (Fowler's Role Subtype advice) and keep clients simple.
Exactly one role is active at a time and clients should not see it: a State object gives the same implementation with a simpler, hidden interface.
You only need to add unforeseen behaviour to individual objects: Extension Object or a language-native mixin/extension mechanism expresses that intent more directly.
Roles are really status data with no distinct interface: model them as an enum or state field instead of building role classes.

The language natively attaches behaviour per object (Ruby modules, JavaScript mixins, Python attribute injection) and no uniform role protocol is needed: use the local mechanism instead of a registry.
anti_patterns: Role Object by default: applying the machinery where a fixed role set would be simpler, even though the pattern's authors explicitly warn that it must not be treated as the only solution.
Client-side type tests: scattered instanceof, dynamic_cast or type-assertion cascades that replace polymorphic role interfaces with a growing switch over concrete roles.
Duplicated core state inside roles: each role keeps its own copy of shared attributes, so the subject loses conceptual identity and the copies drift apart.
Orphan roles: role objects created by clients or kept alive after their core is gone, producing dangling core references, stale views and (in manual-memory languages) double deletion.
Role map as property bag: using the role registry for arbitrary key/value attachments rather than context-specific interfaces, which is Abstract Document or Type Object, not Role Object.
design_principles: Favour composition over inheritance: a role is a delegated object, not a subclass with its own identity.
Separation of concerns: context-specific state and behaviour belong to role classes, while the key abstraction keeps only shared state and the role protocol.
Open/closed principle: new roles enter through specification-keyed creators without touching the core.
Interface segregation: each context gets a narrow role interface instead of the key abstraction carrying every client's operations.
Encapsulation and conceptual integrity: role creation is hidden inside the core, roles cannot exist independently, and one logical object keeps one identity.
best_practices: Keep the role protocol minimal and on the core only (add/get/remove/test by specification); ConcreteRole subclasses must not override the inherited role-management operations.
Let the core create roles through a trader/registry keyed by specification (class object, string, enum) so the core never statically references concrete role classes.

Give the core single ownership of its roles: create, return and destroy roles through the core, and break the core-role cycle deliberately (weak reference, arena or explicit destruction) in manual-memory and reference-counted environments.
Keep shared state on the core and role-specific state on the role; when a core attribute changes, notify or flag the roles that depend on it.
Provide identity operations on the Component interface so clients can test whether two technical objects are the same logical subject (compare their cores).
Model role combination rules explicitly (prerequisite roles, allowed transitions) and enforce them in the core's role protocol rather than in clients.
sources: Baumer, Riehle, Siberski & Wulf, "Role Object", Proceedings of PLoP '97 (Technical Report WUCS-97-34), revised in Pattern Languages of Program Design 4, ch. 2, Addison-Wesley 2000, pp. 15-32.
